chapter_theme: The opening of Idaikkadar's songs, cast as the talk of two cowherds. Thandavaraya Konar tells his fellow herdsman that worlds come from Siva's word, that the Brahman shining like the sky must be known as the void, that release needs worship, tapas and love held night and day; Narayana Konar answers that taming the mind, killing anger and killing desire are only steps, that attachment must be cut while a little desire for Brahman is kept, that the unheard Veda is heard when the guru speaks, and that cattle, gold and kin do not stay.
structure_note: 1732 is the invocation (காப்பு). 1733 to 1742 are Thandavaraya Konar's kannis, each closing on the refrain கோனாரே (herdsman) and most framed as a condition, 'unless you do this, that will not come'. 1743 and 1744 are two kochchakam verses in which Narayana Konar speaks in the first person; 1745 to 1754 are his couplets to தாண்டவக்கோனே, which is at once the other cowherd's name and 'the dancer-king', so each line is also addressed to Siva; 1755 and 1756 are a kattalaikkalithurai and a venba that close the section. The herding setting shows in the images: driving sheep at the hour of thought (1741), the mind as a bull, anger as a snake, desire as a cow (1745 to 1747).

1732.reading: Let us hold with love in the mind the Primal One, who has neither beginning nor end, so that evil-bringing birth is struck down like cotton touched by fire, with the three faculties brought into one accord.
1732.nuance: முப்பொறி, the three faculties, are named in 1781 as mind, speech and body. The syntax of lines 2 and 3 is compressed: birth is what burns like cotton, and the three faculties are what must agree for the thought to be made; the verse is a vow, not a petition.

1733.reading: All worlds, all lives and all things come to be by the word of the mighty one beyond count, the primal supreme Siva.
1733.nuance: Creation is by சொல், the word, not by act or by maya; the verse makes Siva's utterance the sole cause, as 1800 makes his thought (எண்ணப்படி) the plan.

1734.reading: Unless you know and praise the Brahman that shines like the sky as the void, there is no way for the soul housed in flesh; consider this, herdsman.
1734.nuance: சூனியம் here is not nothingness but the name under which Brahman is to be known: what has no form or mark, like the sky it is compared to. The verse makes this knowing a condition of the soul's passage (கதி), so the void is a positive object of praise, not a denial.

1735.reading: Unless you worship the Form that is the seed of release and do the firm acts that lead to release, siddhi, bhakti, sakti and mukti will not come together.
1735.nuance: The four rhyming attainments are listed as one bundle that arrives together or not at all; siddhi (power) and bhakti are not ranked against release. முத்திக்கு உறுதிகள், the firm acts for release, are left unspecified; the surrounding verses supply tapas, thought and love.

1736.reading: Unless, with the bond of the old round of births cut away, you shake off sloth and do tapas, reckon that you have no strength to reach the limitless God.
1736.nuance: The order is notable: the bond (தொந்தம்) of birth is to be cut 'entirely' (அறவே) before tapas, and tapas then gives the strength (பலம்) to reach God; sloth, சோம்பல், is named as the one obstacle.

1737.reading: Think fully, with love and with good nature, on the root of the Vedas, the form of supreme bliss, and rest in the awakening of true knowledge.
1737.nuance: ஆரண மூலம், the root of the Vedas, is the Lord as the source of scripture rather than scripture itself; the verse pairs love (அன்பு) and character (பண்பு) as the manner of thinking, and knowledge (மெய்ஞ்ஞானப் போதம்) as its end.

1738.reading: To see in the inner gaze the light that passes beyond time and all its ages, the wonder beyond imagining, the subtle thing the great ones of the books have spoken: that is the task, herdsman.
1738.nuance: The verse does not reject books: the subtle thing is what the learned great ones said, but it is to be caught in the gaze (நோக்கம்), not in their words. காலாகாலம் may be 'time and the timeless' or 'time and death-time'; either way the light stands past it.

1739.reading: If, without putting into words the ineffable one who is both with form and without form, you keep him within night and day, will Death come near you?
1739.nuance: சகளம் and நிட்களம் are the Agamic pair, the Lord with form and the Lord formless; the verse names him as both at once (ஆனதை). The instruction is to hold him 'without saying by saying' (சொல்லினாற் சொல்லாமல்), an inward holding past speech, and the reward is that Antaka, Death, cannot approach.

1740.reading: As pure dew dies when struck by the sun's blade, fierce deeds are ground to dust when one praises in the heart the feet of the Lord who has the woman on his left side, and one reaches the good abode.
1740.nuance: நாரி இடப்பாகன் is Ardhanarisvara, the Lord whose left half is the goddess; the printed text has நாறி. The verse makes praise of the feet, not knowledge or yoga, the solvent of karma.

1741.reading: To remove the three impurities, keep in thought, even at the hour when you drive the sheep, the triple void that lies beyond the reach of the three faculties.
1741.nuance: The sense turns on முப்பாழ். An editor's gloss takes it as the three mayas (bindu, mohini and maan, the pure, mixed and impure maya); in Tirumular the three voids are the states past speech where the soul comes to rest, and 1734 has just named Brahman as the void. On either reading the verse asks the herdsman to hold a nothing in mind while at work, so that the three malas fall away. செம்மறி ஓட்டிய வேலை, the time of driving the sheep, is the cowherd's working day.

1742.reading: So that agitation in its five kinds flies away, hold with love in the heart that which stands free of all attachment, and cherish it night and day.
1742.nuance: The fivefold agitation (பஞ்ச விதமாய்ச் சஞ்சலம்) is most naturally the unrest that comes through the five senses. The remedy is a reversal of attachment: hold (பற்றி) the one who is without holding (பற்றற்று), a turn the Kural also makes.

1743.reading: Narayana Konar vows to live keeping always and straight in his heart the glorious tender shoot of Siva, the clear nectar and red honey, the heavenly thing that is earth and the other elements, the one that became the five forms, the great light of the sky, the ocean of great bliss.
1743.nuance: The epithets move from the tasted (nectar, honey) to the cosmic (the elements, the five forms) to the inner (light, bliss); the Lord is both the sweetness in things and the things themselves. 'Straight' (நேராக) and 'every day' (எந்நாளும்) make the holding a constant practice.

1744.reading: Narayana Konar says he will attain likeness to the Lord (சாரூபம்) by holding within the pupil of the eye, the wish-tree, the gold, the one whose half is a woman's form, the three things hard to speak of, the sky's nectar, the lamp's light, the hot sun and the cool grace.
1744.nuance: சாரூபம், taking the Lord's own form, is the third of the four graded states of release, so the claim is high but not the highest. முப்பொருள், the three things, is unexplained; tradition would supply pati, pasu and pasam, or the three gods. The list sets the hot sun beside the cool grace as one object, the Lord as both.

1745.reading: Thandavakkona, do not think release has been won merely because the bull called the mind has been brought under.
1745.nuance: The first of three couplets that name a herdsman's victory and deny it is the goal: the tamed bull, the dead snake, the slain cow. The address தாண்டவக்கோனே is the fellow cowherd and also the dancer-king, so the warning is spoken as if before Siva.

1746.reading: Thandavakkona, do not think that everything is accomplished because the snake called anger has died.
1746.nuance: சித்தி here is accomplishment rather than the eight powers; the end of anger is a real death of a real snake, but not the whole.

1747.reading: Thandavakkona, if the cow called desire is slain, you will see and know this whole cosmos.
1747.nuance: Unlike the two before it, this couplet promises rather than warns: desire's death is the decisive one, and its fruit is sight of the whole egg of the world. For a herdsman to kill the cow is the strongest image available; and பசு is also the bound soul, so the line can be heard as the end of the soul's bound state.

1748.reading: Thandavakkona, before it is absorbed into sound, see and know the root Omkara.
1748.nuance: What is to be absorbed (அடங்கும்) is not named: the life-breath at death, the mind in meditation, or the senses in the inner sound are all possible, and the root Om is to be known before that absorption, so that it is known rather than merely undergone. The order, Om before sound, is the reverse of the usual descent from Om into nada.

1749.reading: Thandavakkona, so that the root portion is cut away, pull up the root that has sprouted in the heart.
1749.nuance: மூலப் பகுதி is most likely mula prakriti, the root matter of the tattva scheme from which the inner faculties grow; the verse then asks that the growth in the heart be pulled out by the root so that the root itself is gone. A plainer reading is that the root is desire or the ego, planted in the mind.

1750.reading: Thandavakkona, discern and know that the nature of this pot of a body is in truth that of a jar of filth.
1750.nuance: கடம் is the pot and சால் the jar: the body is a vessel and what it holds is மலம், excrement, here in its plain sense rather than the three impurities. The line is a standard renouncer's image put in the herdsman's mouth.

1751.reading: Thandavakkona, attachment is what belongs to all who have taken birth; do not hold to it but cut it off.
1751.nuance: The first half can be read as 'attachment is the lot of the born' or as 'attachment is the cause of those who are born'; either way it ties பற்று to பிறப்பு, and the remedy is to cut rather than to loosen. The next couplet makes the one exception.

1752.reading: Thandavakkona, a little desire for Brahman you must keep within you, without wavering.
1752.nuance: After the order to cut attachment comes the one desire that is kept, and kept small (சற்றே) and steady (சலியாமல்): the pair reproduces the Kural's turn of clinging to the unclinging one in order to let go of clinging.

1753.reading: Thandavakkona, a roasted seed will not sprout; those without devotion will not reach the goal.
1753.nuance: The roasted seed is usually the image of karma made barren by knowledge, so that it cannot sprout into rebirth; here it is turned on the devotionless, who are the seed that will not grow. The verse makes bhakti the condition of attainment, where 1736 made it tapas.

1754.reading: Thandavakkona, the Veda that the ear has never heard becomes plain when the guru speaks it, does it not?
1754.nuance: The unheard Veda (செவிதனிற் கேளாத மறை) is not the recited text but the secret it stands for; it is revealed in the guru's speech (செப்பில்), an oral transmission set above hearing the books.

1755.reading: Cattle, houses, children and kin, high goods, home, gems, silver, gold and bronze, forests and river banks, stone ornaments, elephants and horses, the many wares one seeks: none stays; join the way of Siva.
1755.nuance: The list begins with cattle (மாடு), the cowherd's own wealth, and ends in the shopkeeper's பண்டம், wares; the one verb is நில்லா, they do not stand. சிவகதி, the Siva-way or Siva-state, is the only thing offered in their place.

1756.reading: Enjoyment goes, experience goes, eating goes, meanness goes, infatuation goes, fierceness goes, ruin goes and thirst goes, when one reaches the Brahman which the Vedas and then the Agamas repeatedly declare the highest.
1756.nuance: The eight things that go (போம்) are mixed: pleasures and even eating stand beside meanness and delusion, so what ends is not vice alone but the whole life of experience. The printed பிரமரத்து is read as பிரமத்து, Brahman; the gloss on போக்கியம் as experience is followed.

links.note: Both name the Supreme as a void: Idaikkadar tells the herdsman to know Brahman as சூனியம், and Sivavakkiyar says that for devotees ripe in love the one in the Supreme is பாழ். Both make the void the object of devotion, not its negation.

Idaikkadar says that without tapas there is no strength to reach God; Tirumular says no tapas is needed to make the mind Siva if one has the fellowship of those already in Siva's bliss. The conflict stands on the plain reading of 1644, that company can replace tapas; it softens if 1644's last line, that the mind becoming Siva is the fruit of tapas done, is taken to mean tapas was done earlier.

Both claim escape from death through practice: the Kural says leaping past death is possible for those who have gained the power of tapas; Idaikkadar asks whether Antaka can approach one who holds the ineffable Lord within night and day.

Both place the முப்பாழ், the triple void, beyond speech and the faculties as the thing to dwell in: Tirumular locates the final experience in the three voids where words cease, and Idaikkadar asks the herdsman to keep the triple void beyond the three faculties in thought. An editor's gloss on 1741 takes the term as the three mayas instead.

The same reversal of attachment: the Kural says cling to the clinging of the one without clinging in order to let clinging go, and Idaikkadar says hold (பற்றி) with love the one who stands free of attachment (பற்றற்று) so that agitation flies off.

Tirumular says that when the mind becomes Siva, siddhi and release follow; Idaikkadar warns that the mind merely brought under, like a tamed bull, is not yet release. The warning draws a line between a subdued mind and a mind become Siva.

Both make the death of desire the decisive step: the Kural says giving up craving at once gives a nature that never shifts, and Idaikkadar says that when the cow called desire is slain one sees and knows the whole cosmos, where taming the mind and killing anger (1745, 1746) were not enough.
The body as a vessel of filth: the Naladiyar's pot that seeps from nine openings, which the fool mistakes for a beauty, and Idaikkadar's body-pot whose nature is a jar of excrement.

Idaikkadar, having ordered attachment cut (1751), keeps one small unwavering desire for Brahman; the Kural keeps one clinging, to the one without clinging, as the means of letting the rest go. Both admit a single desire as the lever against desire.

Both set the guru's spoken word above the written or heard scripture: Sivavakkiyar tells the mutes bewildered at the womb-gate to mark the word the guru spoke, and Idaikkadar says the Veda no ear has heard becomes plain when the guru speaks it.

The same inventory of what will not last: Sivavakkiyar's cattle, calves, wealth, wife and children in the mansion when Death's messengers strike, and Idaikkadar's cattle, houses, children, kin, gold and horses that do not stay. Idaikkadar adds the alternative, the way of Siva.

Both deny that wealth lasts; the Naladiyar argues it from the rich man who comes to beg gruel, Idaikkadar from a list of twenty possessions with the single verb 'they do not stand'. The Naladiyar's chapter draws the lesson of giving; Idaikkadar draws that of joining the Siva-way.

Both list what falls away on attainment: Tirumular says recitation, desire, dying and wandering are no longer needed once the Life of life is within, and Idaikkadar says enjoyment, eating, meanness, delusion and thirst all go when one reaches Brahman. Idaikkadar's list is of experiences that end, Tirumular's of practices that become needless.

source_issues: 1740 line 3 prints நாறி where the sense and the gloss require நாரி (woman): நாரி இடப்பாகன், the Lord with the woman on his left.
1756 line 4 prints ஓதுபிர மரத்துஉற்றக் கால்; the sense requires பிரமத்து (Brahman), and the extra letter looks like a print error or a word broken for the metre.
